The proposed answer of 1/2 is not correct, and the construction it relies on is invalid.

**The construction fails the boundary condition.** The pattern holes at $x \equiv y \pmod 3$ puts holes at $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$. These two unit squares meet only at the vertex $(1,1)$, so their boundary curves intersect. The problem forbids this, so the pattern does not satisfy the hypothesis.

**Valid holes must be king-separated.** Since two holes cannot share any boundary point, no two holes can be adjacent horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. Hence the holes form an independent set in the king graph, which has density at most $1/4$.

**A valid construction gives 1/3.** Take holes at $(2i, 2j)$ and let $P$ be all other cells. Each hole is a single cell with all eight surrounding cells in $P$. The set $P$ is connected because the odd rows and odd columns form a connected grid of lines. Holes have density $1/4$ and $P$ has density $3/4$, so the ratio is $(1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3$. This gives $\liminf h_n/n \ge 1/3$.

**The value 1/2 is not reachable.** Each hole needs its eight king-neighbours in $P$. Each cell of $P$ lies in at most four holes' neighbourhoods, so $P \ge 2H$, which only gives the bound $1/2$. Equality would require almost every $P$-cell to have four diagonal holes. But a cell with four diagonal holes forces its orthogonal neighbours to have only two holes in their neighbourhoods, so the average incidence stays around $8/3$, matching the $1/3$ construction. The proposed union-find argument is also not a valid bound, since it ignores the king-separation constraint.

I believe the true limit is $1/3$, which matches the construction and the heuristic upper bound, but I have not verified the upper bound rigorously. Either way, $1/2$ is not justified.

VERDICT: REJECT
